segments.text: In the year 1982,
a 25-year-old boy used to go from shop to shop with his homemade chips on a bicycle.
His bicycle was old and his appearance was completely simple,
because of which many shopkeepers did not even look at him,
and they flatly refused to keep his chips in their shops.
At that time, no one would have thought even in a dream
that this very boy would go on to become the wafer king of India,
and that millions of shopkeepers across the country would be compelled to keep his products.
This is the story of Balaji Wafers.
This begins in 1957.
In a small village called Dhundhoraji in Gujarat, Chandubhai Virani was born.
His village was so backward that there was no electricity supply in any house.
And almost every household depended only on farming.
Life was already quite tough,
and then in 1972, the most severe drought in the past 70 years struck the country.
Because of this, the crops of millions of farming families were destroyed,
and among them was the family of Chandubhai Virani.
His family was completely ruined,
and that is why Chandubhai’s father had to harden his heart
and sell their ancestral land for ₹20000.
He then divided this money equally among his three sons.
With ₹600 and his two brothers, 17-year-old Chandubhai set out towards Rajkot.
His plan was to start a small fertiliser business in the city.
But even here his luck turned out to be terrible.
The supplier scammed him by giving duplicate and counterfeit fertilisers.
His business shut down even before it could start, and his entire investment was lost.
Chandubhai was literally on the road.
But still, one thing was clear in his mind.
Whatever happened, he could not return to his village empty-handed.
He could not let his father’s head bow down in shame.
That is why he began desperately searching for work in Rajkot.
And in this way one day he reached Astron Cinema.
There, he got a job with a salary of only ₹90 a month.
For Chandubhai, this was not about earning but about learning.
That is why he did whatever work he was told to do.
Putting up posters of films, doorkeeping, ticket checking, cleaning,
and even repairing torn seats — he did everything.
Fortunately, he received a big reward for this.
The owner of the cinema was impressed with his work
and gave him the contract for the cinema canteen at ₹1000 per month.
This meant Chandubhai had to pay ₹1000 monthly,
and in return the entire profit from the canteen would be his.
In the canteen, Chandubhai mainly sold masala sandwiches,
potato wafers (i.e. chips), and beverages.
Within a few weeks, he observed an important thing.
Eighty per cent of the canteen’s sales were coming from just one item,
and that item was potato chips.
Also, maximum sales happened only during those 10 to 15 minutes
when the movie’s interval occurred.
But many times the chips suppliers either delivered late or supplied in low quantity.
Because of insufficient stock during the interval, Chandubhai incurred losses.
After dealing with this problem for nearly six years,
in 1982 Chandubhai made a decision that was going to change his life.
He decided that he would now make potato wafers himself.
Making chips himself meant having control over both quality and quantity,
plus the profit margin would also be higher.
Near Astron Cinema there was a Hanuman temple,
and inspired by it he named his wafers brand “Balaji Wafers.”
In this new venture, Chandubhai invested ₹10,000
and first built a small shed in the compound of his house.
He saw that industrial potato peeling and cutting machines were very expensive.
So he improvised, bought the parts separately,
and himself assembled a machine for ₹5000.
The remaining money went into buying a kadai and other equipment.
Their production process was completely basic.
In the same room, peeling, cutting, frying, and packaging of potatoes all took place.
Chandubhai managed the canteen during the day
and at night came home and fried the wafers himself.
To save labour costs, the entire family was involved in this process.
Years of working in the canteen had taught him one thing about customers
— for them, the most important factor was value for money.
Basically, they wanted the maximum wafers at the minimum price.
That is why from the very beginning Chandubhai offered 25 to 30% extra chips compared to competitors.
And as for taste, his and his brothers’ whole life had been spent in Gujarat,
so they were well aware of customers’ taste preferences.
Initially, Chandubhai sold chips only in Astron Cinema’s canteen.
But when the response was good, he resolved to scale up.
Outside Astron Cinema, he first got the contract to supply wafers to a girls’ high school canteen,
and then he started supplying chips to 25–30 local shopkeepers in Rajkot.
But the problem was that when he went to these shopkeepers on his bicycle,
they treated him like a beggar.
But enduring this disrespect only made him more resilient.
Apart from this, there was another problem — quality.
Most of their processes were still manual.
So when they increased production quantity,
quality consistency went down.
Plus, there were issues in packaging,
because of which complaints of chips turning stale began to come in from many places.
Before moving ahead, I want to talk about you.
You are watching my videos.

And today in 2025, one thing is absolutely clear.
If a business has to be run effectively, then the business has to be made digital.
But the problem is that even today many businesses in India are working in the old way.
They calculate every customer’s bill manually.
They get to know that the stock is finished
only when the customer comes in front and demands.
And at the end of the day, hours are spent preparing the whole day’s account.
Because of this, both time and money are lost.

To deal with the issues of quality,
Chandubhai decided to make himself an expert in potato wafers manufacturing.
For example, he realised that in an average potato around 80 to 85% is only water,
and the more dry matter there is in a potato, the better its wafer will be.
Ideally, the dry matter should be 20 to 23%.
With experience, Chandubhai could identify just by holding a potato in his hand
how suitable it was for making chips.
In the same way, he understood the ideal thickness of slices to make crisp wafers.
What should be the temperature of the oil.
For how long the wafer should be fried.
How the potato should be washed.
Which spices and how much of them should be added.
In all of these, he became an expert.
But he knew that only he becoming an expert would not be enough.
He would have to do something so that his method and process of making wafers
could be replicated on a mass scale.
That is why, taking the biggest risk so far, he took a loan of ₹50 lakh
and set up his first semi-automatic wafers manufacturing plant.
The area of the plant was 1000 square meters
and the daily manufacturing capacity was 60 kg of wafers.
With this plant, his hope was to achieve better consistent quality and branded packaging.
The scene was really set to take the company to the next level,
when suddenly a very big twist came into the story.
Generally, these manufacturing plants are set up by a third-party company.
Meaning, according to the requirements of the client, which in this case was Balaji Wafers,
the third party handles the design of the plant, equipment sourcing, installation,
testing, and even maintenance.
The client only has to operate it later.
Now, in the case of Balaji Wafers, just as their plant was being assembled,
at that very time the company that was setting up the plant shut down.
This meant that the ₹50 lakh was spent,
and they were left with a plant that was neither properly assembled
nor customised according to their requirements.
In such a situation, if Chandubhai had not done something quickly,
there were chances that he would have become bankrupt.
That is why, along with his brothers,
he started dismantling each equipment and trying to understand it.
Through trial and error, they understood the working of the plant
and basically became self-taught engineers.
Ultimately, they themselves fixed the machines, and production started.
The process of making wafers that Chandubhai had earlier mastered,
that very process he automated through this plant.
Balaji Wafers immediately saw the benefit of this.
Very soon they started supplying to shops in Rajkot and many surrounding areas.
The issues of packaging and quality became almost negligible.
And after this, one belief of Chandubhai became even stronger
that investment in machines, equipment, and technology is the best investment.
That is why in 1995 he set up another semi-automatic plant,
and in 2002 he set up a fully automated factory
which at that time was the largest potato chips factory in the whole of India.
By giving better quantity, quality, and packaging at a lower price,
they started beating not only unbranded chips but also branded chips.
In fact, by 2006, they had captured 90% market share in Gujarat and had become number one.
But Chandubhai did not want to remain only a regional player of Gujarat.
He wanted to expand the business into more states,
and he knew that for this, he would need a revolution in every department, such as product, marketing, and HR.
Until now, his hero product was their masala wafers.
But he knew that for expansion, he would have to make new products.
That is why he set up an R&D lab.
Here, he identified such food items to which Indians were used,
and then, inspired by the recipes of those very items, he made his new wafer products.
For example, he took inspiration from Indian chaat and created his Chaat Chaska wafers.
In the same way, inspired by the banana chips made in Indian homes,
he made his own banana wafers.
But he did not remain limited only to wafers.
He saw that the Indian namkeen market was not only already big but also growing rapidly.
Plus, he saw that where one of his competitors, Lays, was focusing only on chips,
his other competitor, Haldiram’s, was focusing mainly on namkeen.
That is why he decided that Balaji would become India’s first such major brand
that would offer both chips and namkeen under one brand.
His namkeen product strategy covered multiple states.
For example, they offered Gujarati khakhra, Ratlami sev, Punjabi tadka, and classic sev.
Finally, to target the young generation, he launched Western snacks
such as Poprings, Nachos, and even products similar to Kurkure.
The names of these products were also given, specifically keeping the young generation in mind.
Like Wheelos, Amaize, and Yumstix.
Even to compete with Maggi and Yippee, he launched their Gippi Masala Noodles.
Basically, whatever the customer’s age or taste,
Balaji Wafers definitely had a product offering for them.
Also, before launching every new product,
he would invite a small sample of his target customers to their lab.
He made them taste their product and took detailed feedback from them in a feedback form.
And on the basis of this feedback, he kept improving their products.
But Balaji Wafers knew that merely making a good product does not bring sales.
Sales come when you can convey the speciality of your product to your customer.
And here comes into the picture their genius marketing strategy.
Balaji knew that their biggest competitor was Lay’s.
And the biggest weakness of Lay’s was its lower quantity.
Even in memes and in normal conversation,
the low quantity and extra air in Lay’s packets were made fun of.
Targeting this weakness, Balaji Wafers created their messaging:
“Less air, more wafers, and rich flavours.”
“Because it has less air, more wafers, and rich flavours.”
With this message, they mocked the low quantity of Lay’s,
clearly conveyed their message of higher quantity,
and finally also clearly talked about their wide variety of flavours.
Also, their ads were quite light-hearted and engaging.
Because of this, their message quickly reached crores of people.
Apart from this, Balaji Wafers found a smart way to make their regular customers try their new products.
They simply put a simple CTA on the backside of every item’s packaging.
Basically, they put an image of their new product and asked the customer to try it.
As far as production strategy is concerned,
with time, he kept setting up bigger and more high-tech plants.
Today in his plants, potato washing, slicing, frying, seasoning, and packaging happen automatically.
Also, everyone knows that the most important raw material for making wafers is potatoes.
And potato prices fluctuate according to seasons,
because of which it becomes difficult to control production costs.
Plus, due to irregular monsoon, the potato crop can also get spoiled,
because of which there can be a danger of supply being completely stopped.
That is why he built a cold storage of 25,000 tons
so that they could buy potatoes at cheap prices and stock them for the whole year.
The HR strategy of Balaji Wafers is also absolutely unique.
Here no department is given any targets,
because Chandubhai believes that when employees feel ownership,
then they truly believe that this company is theirs,
and in such a situation, they themselves give their best.
Also, every employee has Chandubhai’s personal number,
whether he is a factory worker or a manager,
so that they feel that no matter what happens, Chandubhai is with them.
Finally, in hiring, more than the resume, passion and attitude are looked at.
But the success of Balaji is not only because of their marketing, product, or HR strategy,
but also because of their unique values and principles.
When in 2023, Pepsi offered to buy Balaji Wafers for ₹4000 crore,
he rejected the offer and made the decision to remain an independent Indian brand.
When a fire broke out in Haldiram’s Noida factory,
for many months, Balaji Wafers made Haldiram’s products in their own factory
even though Haldiram’s was their competitor.
He never thought of hastily expanding all across India at once.
He always expanded one state at a time
because for him, quality was the most important, and his thinking was long-term.
Today, the products of Balaji Wafers are found in lakhs of shops in India.
Their Made in India products are exported to more than 25 countries around the world.
And today, Balaji Wafers has become an empire with an annual revenue of ₹5000 crore.
But the most inspiring thing is that this entire empire was started by a boy
who used to go around on a bicycle selling chips.
This was the story of Balaji Wafers.
